abstract: TLAPS-Bench is a benchmark and execution harness for constructing machine-checked proofs for real-world system specifications in TLA+ with agentic AI. Proving correctness of complex system specifications requires discovering inductive invariants, reasoning about intricate state transitions, and decomposing proofs into tractable obligations. TLAPS-Bench provides a proof harness that supports iterative proof development atop the TLA+ Proof System (TLAPS), where agents are equipped with proof tools and libraries, with safeguards against reward hacking. Using the harness, we have employed AI agents to prove desired properties for important system specifications that were not proved before, spanning cache coherence, Byzantine consensus, and write-ahead logs. TLAPS-Bench contains 265 proof targets (each encodes a property to prove) from 95 TLA+ specifications of real-world systems. We evaluated frontier AI agents, represented by Codex with GPT models, on a subset of 70 proof targets across 12 specifications. The highest-scoring model, GPT-6.1 Sol (max), proved 31 (44.3%) proof targets. The results show challenges and opportunities in end-to-end proof development.

sections.body: The section argues that existing benchmarks mostly supply helper lemmas, invariants, or proof decompositions, or use research artifacts such as those built on IronKV, so they miss end-to-end proof construction. It introduces TLAPS-Bench, which contains 95 specifications and 265 proof targets, and Tilapia, a proof harness built on TLAPS that gives agents tools including model checkers and proof libraries. Tilapia also enforces safeguards against reward hacking. The authors evaluate a subset of 70 targets, where GPT-6.1 Sol at max effort successfully proves 31 (44.3%). The stated limits are that success depends on invariant choice and decomposition, and that naive calls to automated backends are ineffective.
sections.heading: Introduction
sections.headline: TLAPS-Bench tests whether AI agents can build end-to-end machine-checked TLA+ proofs for real-world system specifications.

sections.body: The section defines a TLA+ specification as a state machine with an initial predicate and a next-state relation, plus safety and liveness properties. The model checkers TLC and Apalache explore finite or bounded models and can falsify conjectures, but their guarantees stop at the configured bounds. TLAPS proves a target by generating proof obligations and dispatching them to backends such as Z3, Isabelle/TLA+, and LS4. Agents may use the checkers, but a target is accepted only when TLAPS verifies the proof. The Figure 2 example from etcd Raft proves LeaderUniqueness through a stronger inductive invariant that records quorum votes and single-candidate voting.
sections.heading: Background
sections.headline: TLA+ theorems are accepted only when TLAPS verifies the proof, while model checkers help test candidate invariants.

sections.body: Tilapia runs coding agents such as Codex and Claude Code inside Docker containers, with pinned SANY, TLAPS, TLC, and Apalache, plus the TLAPS library. Agents may use the same checker as final grading. A proof is accepted only if it keeps the original specification and targets read-only, uses only definitions, named lemmas, and imports, and depends only on lemmas that are themselves proved, tracked by a dependency graph built with SANY. Grading runs in a fresh container with the original task files and unmodified tools, carrying over only the submitted module. Fixed verification time limits and CPU quotas keep runs consistent, and interrupted runs can resume from cached results.
sections.heading: Tilapia: TLA+ Proof Harness
sections.headline: Tilapia gives agents proof tools and blocks cheating by making targets read-only and grading in a clean container.

sections.body: A task asks for a proof of a target property or a counterexample that disproves it. Targets cover safety, liveness, and refinement. Construction turns explicit properties, model-checking invariants, or requirements stated in comments into theorems of the form Spec => P, and removes existing proofs of those targets. Specifications may be rewritten, for example by making assumptions explicit or by translating from Ivy. During construction the authors found 46 specification issues, of which 35 have been fixed. Validation needs no test cases: a target is either proved or refuted by a counterexample, and the guarantee is relative to TLAPS and its backends. Tasks the frontier proves are retired.
sections.heading: TLAPS-Bench
sections.headline: The benchmark holds 95 specifications and 265 targets, and evaluation uses an active set of 70 targets from 12 specifications.

sections.body: Pass@3 gives GPT-6.1 Sol at max effort 44.3% and GPT-6 Astra at max 42.9%. GPT-5.6 Terra and GPT-6 Luna prove fewer targets at max effort and none at high or low effort. Astra and Sol both proved all 15 FLASH targets, and Sol proved all OpenAddressing targets, while Sol proved none of the ZooKeeper protocol targets. Failure analysis counts 537 undecomposed proof attempts, where agents hand a whole target to a backend, and 1,455 incomplete proofs, where invariants were not strong enough. Only Terra and Luna at max effort reached the two-million-token limit, and they did not finish. No model completed the Wildfire refinement proof at any effort level. Every model reached its highest success rate at max effort.
sections.heading: Evaluation
sections.headline: GPT-6.1 Sol at max effort proved 31 of 70 targets (44.3%), and all models failed on Wildfire refinement.

sections.body: The section groups related work into software verification benchmarks and TLA+ benchmarks. Most verification benchmarks, such as DafnyBench, AutoVerus, Selene, and FVELer, give agents parts of the proof. The no-lemma modes of Vero and VeruSAGE-Bench focus on functional properties of functions, APIs, or modules. Most TLA+ benchmarks generate specifications from code or natural language. LMGPA evaluates proof decomposition but supplies inductive invariants to agents. TLA-Verus works on Verus translations of TLA+ specifications. The authors state that TLA-Verus misunderstands TLAPS, which decomposes proofs and dispatches obligations to backends including LS4.
sections.heading: Related Work
sections.headline: Prior benchmarks mostly supply proof structure, and the closest TLA+ benchmark supplies inductive invariants to agents.

sections.body: The section restates that TLAPS-Bench and Tilapia provide infrastructure for agents to build formal proofs of TLA+ system specifications. Proof construction discovers inductive invariants and lemmas, and can expose unexpected behaviors or weaknesses in stated properties. The authors propose that agents recover high-level designs and establish refinement across successive abstraction layers, and that specifications and proofs could become durable representations of system design. The section presents this as a direction. It reports no experiments on abstraction layers.
sections.heading: Conclusion and Discussion
sections.headline: Abstraction and refinement across layers are expected to scale proofs, as AI lowers the cost of formal proofs.

sections.body: The appendix discloses that OpenAI Codex with GPT-6 Astra and GPT-6.1 Sol assisted with software, evaluation scripts, and paper editing, and that the authors reviewed all AI-assisted output. Appendix A lists 195 retired targets, which the authors say can no longer challenge the frontier models. Appendix B gives per-target results in Table A2 and pass@3 and resource tables A3 to A14. Appendix D describes specification fixes, including a SlateDB WAL model bug disproved with a 58-transition counterexample and an etcd Raft theorem corrected to use the committed term. Appendix E reproduces the `etcd_raft.tla` proof prompt and two agent skills.
sections.heading: Appendix
sections.headline: The appendix lists the retired problem set, per-target results, specification fixes with counterexamples, and the agent prompt and skills.
